  • Boot from USB.
  • Get the network up and running.
  • Create an encrypted LUKS volume (I want full drive encryption).
  • Create the LVM volumes as I see fit.
  • Set up the GPT boot.
  • Install the base packages.
  • Install Xorg
  • Install XFCE4
  • Set XFCE4 to start at boot time.
  • Install a clipboard manager.

Is there anything else, any very obvious basic requirement, that I'm missing to get a basic working environment up and running? My first Arch install... can anyone do a check over to see if I'm missing anything?

Really quickly as I don't have much time: my experiment with Arch Linux went well... for a while. I installed it and used it as my primary Linux Desktop on my development machine at work (I'm a software developer). After about a year, however, I had some serious conflicts when updating the Kernel which had all kinds of issues with some of the drivers and versioning. Rolling back to a stable state would have been simple had I opted to use LVM with snapshots but alas I did not so I had to nuke the machine and I went back to Ubuntu (time is essential when at work so I had little choice).

TL;DR - use LVM with Snapshots... you'll be happy you did. Good luck.

Edit: came back to add that you may want to configure sudo on your system and also setup yaourt which can make adding some packages with dependencies a little simpler in some cases (you'll still need to use pacman directly in other situations)
Thanks for the tips! Out of curiosity, were you messing around with custom kernel builds or did this arise out of Arch's own kernel packages?

It was a video drivers related issue. The driver initially used was no longer in use and had known issues. It was non functioning with the Kernel upgrade. The error was more or less unavoidable had I used more discretion when choosing "yes/no" responses at the prompts/warnings during the upgrade process. Moral of the story - Arch requires attention to details and is very hands on, and have backup plans if you use it. At home this would have been fine for me bit at work I had to get stuff done so I didn't have time to dedicate to those things.

Fair enough. The purpose of me using LVM is indeed for the snapshots. On my work laptop I have no need for the volume resizing or spanning across several disks but the snapshotting is really a must. Thanks for the advice!

I know that this is quite an old post but this isn't a very active subverse. I just want to offer you an alternative and simpler solution to the possible dangers of using the absolute latest kernel.Install the lts (long term solution) kernel. You can find more information on kernels here.

During that process you'll have to make sure that Grub will still boot you into the latest kernel by default but with the lts kernel installed alongside it, if something goes fucked after an update, boot with the lts kernel instead from Grub (so make sure you always have a way to access Grub during boot).

This sounds like a great suggestion, thanks!

I'm actually using EFI but it should be similar.

What I do wonder is what other kinds of issues this can cause... e.g., modules which are compiled against the latest kernel and which might then fail when running the LTS kernel. Have you ever experienced such an issue?

I also wonder where the -lts kernel package will be installed... since right now I have a /boot/vmlinuz-linux and I wonder if it will be overwriten should I install the -lts package.

In any case I am extremely careful when upgrading my packages. Normally I will create LVM snapshots of both root and home and if I see that the kernel is being upgraded, I also backup my boot partition. So in principle I should always be able to revert but the LTS solution sounds like less trouble in the long run.

It's installed as a completely separate vmlinuz-linux-lts and appears as a separate entry in your bootloader, nothing is overwritten at all besides your boot up settings which will probably put the lts kernel as default after you've installed it. And whenever any kernel needs to update, it updates all of them. Personally I haven't had any need to use it yet but every time I try it, it works completely. It was actually suggested as the solution to this very issue on a page of the Arch Wiki I came across, and no problems with it are mentioned.

If you want to choose it from your EFI boot menu however, that's a bit more tricky because you're probably going to need to install two separate bootloaders for that. It would be much easier to just let grub show up for a couple of seconds so that you can access it from there if you need to.
You can also do the dnscrypt-proxy / pdnsd combo (see the Tips & Tricks section for a config file).
Do yourself a favor and add the yaourt repo to your repo list, it will save you a LOT of time, because chances are, you'll need a bunch of packages found on the AUR
